source.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
source.authors: Geonhee Kim; Marco Valentino; André Freitas

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates syllogism-completion accuracy across model sizes and families, bearing on downstream performance versus scale, but it does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no loss-versus-parameters, tokens, or compute measurements; no small-run loss extrapolations; no compute-optimal allocation; and no tests of architectural effects on loss. Its circuit ablations, patching, and logit-difference results concern syllogistic reasoning mechanisms, not the listed scaling-law versions. Only the reported downstream accuracy comparisons are included as rows for V6.
record.test_reason: This is a mechanistic-interpretability study of a syllogism circuit. Its accuracy-versus-size numbers serve two purposes. The GPT-2 sizes (117M–1.5B) are measured to pick a model for circuit discovery, citing phase transitions (Kaplan; Wei). Table 3 accuracies are capability checks for circuit transfer across families. The study fits no loss curves and makes no claim about predictable downstream scaling. It uses the scale/emergence idea as a selection tool and does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find a middle-term-suppression circuit (long induction, duplication, suppression, mover heads) that is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogisms. It transfers to schemes with accuracy ≥60% and to several sizes and families. Belief biases contaminate it on natural-language inputs, and head contributions grow more complex with size. They draw no conclusions about scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures syllogism-completion accuracy and mechanistic circuit behavior, not held-out cross-entropy loss, power-law fits, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report model- and dataset-dependent accuracy patterns; the Pythia models are described as erratic, and Qwen is reported to show a distinct suppression mechanism.

fits_no_version.finding: Incidental, non-monotonic accuracy on a 90-item syllogism completion task across a few model sizes. Pythia symbolic accuracy is 0.00 at 160M, 0.99 at 410M and 0.30 at 1B. GPT-2 XL shows lower symbolic but higher non-symbolic accuracy (Figure 6, values not given in text).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow-task accuracy across a handful of model sizes can be non-monotonic and dataset-dependent (symbolic vs belief-laden content). The authors attribute this to growing world-knowledge interference.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The accuracy comparisons do not fit a predictive scaling relationship or report uncertainty for the Table 3 accuracy values. Some GPT-2 size results are presented in figures, while the text gives only an aggregate increase and qualitative descriptions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows bearing on V6 were left out. Circuit patching, ablation, logit-difference, and logit-lens findings were not included because they do not measure downstream task performance versus scale.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fitted laws and no extrapolation.
No loss comparison across model shapes at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or regimes; the fine-tuned GPT-2 is analysed for circuit similarity only.
No fitted or predictive relation between scale or loss and downstream accuracy. Size-accuracy numbers are used only for model selection and capability checks.
No exponents and no fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's three V6 labels should be dropped. The size comparisons are a selection step and circuit-transfer capability checks on 90-sample datasets. They come from mixed families trained on different data, with no fit or predictive claim. Treating Pythia's non-monotonicity as a 'challenge' to V6 would overread an incidental result, so it is recorded under fits_no_version instead. The Figure 6 GPT-2 XL accuracy values are not readable in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions and range of scaling.
Prediction of larger-run loss from power-law fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Loss comparisons at fixed parameter count across depth, width, or other architecture choices.
Power-law behavior in other modalities, repeated-data settings, fine-tuning or transfer.

The study measures syllogism-completion accuracy across sizes and families, but does not fit or evaluate a predictive relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance, nor test other downstream tasks.
No scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal splits, fit choices, or departures from fitted loss curves are examined.

rows.measure: Average performance across three datasets; the text does not specify this measure as accuracy in this sentence.
rows.note: The authors describe a marked transition from small to medium; this is an aggregate comparison reported over three datasets.
rows.check: Selection value: the GPT-2 small-to-medium 439.06% increase was measured to choose GPT-2 Medium for circuit analysis. It is an aggregate over three 90-sample datasets with no baseline given, so it is not a test of V6.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The text reports a sharp 439.06% aggregate increase and a phase transition, not a demonstrated smooth or fitted predictive trend (R1).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The reported symbolic accuracy rises to 0.99 at 410M then falls to 0.30 at 1B, and the authors characterize the smallest models' patterns as erratic rather than stable (R2, R5, R8, R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Symbolic and belief-inconsistent accuracies are unchanged across these sizes, while belief-consistent accuracy changes from 0.96 to 0.99; these results do not show a general accuracy increase with size (R17-R22).
